title: HDFN Surveillance: Titers, Anti-K, Anti-G and RhIG Dosing
summary: Follow maternal antibody titers correctly, know why anti-K is judged at lower titers, recognise mild ABO disease and the anti-G impostor, and dose Rh immune globulin from a rosette screen and fetomaternal bleed quantitation.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 40 Hits 4, 10, 15, 18, 22 and 27 and Trap 5. Checked against Hajjaj 2025, Visser 2021 (FIGO/ICM), Valentini 2025, Basu 2011, Jacobs 2025 (anti-K meta-analysis) and Makroo 2015. Hit 10 and Trap 5 say anti-K titers underestimate risk and call for Doppler “regardless of titer”; Jacobs 2025 found 98.6% of severe anti-K HDFN at titers ≥ 8 (register flag rv-antik-titer). Simulator question 372 omits the extra vial added by technical guidance (register flag rv-rhig-vials). Not taught: “anti-C titer ≥ 4× anti-D suggests anti-G,” severe ABO HDFN “~0.04%” (Valentini gives 0.3–0.8% for ABO HDFN overall in Caucasian neonates), and exchange-transfusion bilirubin thresholds.

objectives: Calculate RhIG coverage and state the timing of antenatal and postpartum doses.
Run the HDFN monitoring chain: screen, identify, titer in parallel, critical titer, MCA Doppler.
Explain why anti-K is managed at lower titers and why ABO HDFN is usually mild.
Recognise anti-G and passive anti-D, and quantify fetomaternal hemorrhage after a positive rosette screen.

scenes.title: Two antibodies, two pregnancies
scenes.altText: Two prenatal cards at 16 weeks. Woman A: D-negative, anti-D titer 8, partner D-positive. Woman B: D-positive, transfused after a car crash years ago, anti-K titer 4, partner K-positive. A question token: “Which titer can you trust — and what comes next?” The cartoon scientist holds two titer tubes.

cues.text: Two pregnant women at 16 weeks. Woman A is D-negative with an anti-D titer of 8.
Woman B is D-positive but was transfused after a car crash. She has anti-K with a titer of only 4, and her partner is K-positive.
A titer of 4 sounds reassuring. Is it? The answer depends on what the antibody does to the fetus.

props.label: Which titer can you trust — and what next?

scenes.title: How HDFN starts, and how RhIG prevents it
scenes.altText: A placenta schematic: maternal IgG crosses to the fetus and coats fetal red cells carrying the antigen. A prevention panel for D-negative mothers: one 300 µg (1500 IU) RhIG vial covers 30 mL of fetal whole blood or 15 mL of fetal red cells; antenatal dose (often at 28 weeks) and a postpartum dose within 72 hours of delivering a D-positive baby (if missed, give as soon as recognised, up to 28 days). A note: passive anti-D from RhIG can be detected by IAT for up to about 8 weeks — not the same as immunisation.

cues.text: Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn starts when maternal IgG crosses the placenta and coats fetal red cells that carry the matching antigen.
For anti-D, prevention works. One 300 microgram vial of Rh immune globulin covers 30 millilitres of fetal whole blood, or 15 of fetal red cells.
It is given antenatally, often at 28 weeks, and again within 72 hours of delivering a D-positive baby. If that window is missed, give it as soon as the need is recognised, up to 28 days.
Passive anti-D from the injection shows up in the antibody screen for up to about eight weeks.
That passive antibody is not immunisation. History and a falling titer tell them apart.

scenes.title: Not every antibody behaves like anti-D
scenes.altText: Three antibody cards. Anti-K: destroys red cells and also suppresses fetal erythroid progenitors → earlier, more severe anemia at lower titers; critical titers for anti-K are set lower (a 2025 review table: > 4; a 2025 meta-analysis: ≥ 8 had 97% sensitivity, and 98.6% of severe cases had titers ≥ 8). ABO: almost exclusively group O mothers (IgG anti-A, anti-B) with A or B babies; usually mild because fetal A and B antigens are weakly expressed; DAT may be weak or negative. Anti-G: a D-negative woman who seems to have anti-D + anti-C may have anti-G; differential adsorption and elution separate them; if there is no true anti-D, she still needs RhIG.

cues.text: Anti-K is different. It destroys red cells, but it also attacks the fetal red-cell factory, the erythroid progenitors.
So anemia comes earlier and at lower titers. Critical titers for anti-K are set lower. In a 2025 meta-analysis, 98.6 percent of severe cases had titers of 8 or more.

ABO disease affects almost only babies of group O mothers, who make IgG anti-A and anti-B. It is usually mild, because fetal A and B antigens are weakly expressed. The DAT may even be weak or negative.
Anti-G is the impostor. It reacts with both D and C cells, so it looks like anti-D plus anti-C.
Differential adsorption and elution separate them. If there is no true anti-D, the woman can still be immunised to D and still needs Rh immune globulin.

No true anti-D → still give RhIG

scenes.title: The monitoring chain, from screen to rosette
scenes.altText: A chain of steps. 1: antibody screen at the first visit; D-negative women rescreened at 24–28 weeks. 2: identify the antibody, type the partner or fetus. 3: titer every 4 weeks to ~24 weeks, then every 2 weeks; test the previous frozen sample in parallel; a rise of ≥ 2 dilutions (e.g., 8 → 32) is significant. 4: at the critical titer → MCA peak systolic velocity Doppler; > 1.5 MoM → cordocentesis and possible intrauterine transfusion. 5: after delivery, rosette screen detects ≥ 10 mL fetal whole blood; positive → quantify by Kleihauer–Betke or flow cytometry (most accurate; KB overestimates with high maternal F cells) and add vials. Back to the hook: A keeps titering; B gets close anti-K surveillance, often Doppler-led.

cues.text: Screen every pregnant woman at the first visit, and rescreen D-negative women at 24 to 28 weeks. Identify any antibody and check whether the fetus carries the antigen.
Titer every four weeks until about 24 weeks, then every two. Run the previous frozen sample alongside, because a rise of two or more dilutions, say 8 to 32, is significant.
At the critical titer, switch to middle cerebral artery Doppler. A peak velocity above 1.5 multiples of the median suggests fetal anemia and leads to cordocentesis.

After delivery, the rosette screen detects about 10 millilitres of fetal whole blood. A positive screen is quantified by Kleihauer–Betke or flow cytometry. Divide the bleed by 30, round, and technical guidance adds one more vial.
So woman A keeps titering. Woman B, with anti-K, gets close surveillance, often led by Doppler, because her low titer cannot simply be trusted.

lines: q4 wk → q2 wk after ~24 wk

props.label: A: keep titering · B (anti-K): close, often Doppler-led surveillance

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards appear in turn: “Anti-K titer 4 — reassure the obstetrician” (✓ anti-K suppresses erythropoiesis; follow anti-K protocols with low critical titers or Doppler); “Anti-D 8 → 16 is a significant rise” (✓ one dilution is within test variation; significant = ≥ 2 dilutions, tested in parallel); “Anti-D after a 28-week RhIG dose = immunised, no postpartum RhIG” (✓ passive anti-D lasts up to ~8 weeks; give the postpartum dose).

cues.text: Trap one: an anti-K titer of 4, so reassure the obstetrician. Anti-K suppresses fetal erythropoiesis; follow the anti-K protocol with a low critical titer or Doppler.
Trap two: anti-D going from 8 to 16 is a significant rise. A single dilution step is within test variation. Significant means two or more dilutions, tested in parallel.
Trap three: anti-D after the 28-week injection means she is immunised and needs no postpartum dose. Passive anti-D lasts up to about eight weeks. Give the postpartum dose.

props.title: ✗ “Anti-K titer 4 — reassure.”
lines: ✓ Progenitor suppression: low critical titer or Doppler

props.title: ✗ “Anti-D after 28-week RhIG = immunised.”
lines: ✓ Passive up to ~8 weeks — give postpartum dose

scenes.title: 30-15-72, and Kell kills the factory
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “30-15-72: one vial, 30 mL blood or 15 mL cells, within 72 hours. Kell kills the factory.” A vial token, a clock token and a factory token with a K stamp. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: 30, 15, 72. One vial covers 30 millilitres of fetal blood or 15 of cells, given within 72 hours. And Kell kills the factory.
Where it breaks: a missed 72-hour window is not a reason to skip the dose; large bleeds need more than one vial; and anti-K critical titers differ between guidelines.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Titer q4 → q2 wk · ≥ 2-dilution rise significant · critical titer → MCA Doppler · anti-K: lower threshold”, “RhIG 300 µg = 30 mL WB / 15 mL RBC within 72 h · rosette ≥ 10 mL → KB or flow”.

cues.text: Follow titers in parallel and act on a two-dilution rise or a critical titer, treat anti-K with a lower threshold, and dose Rh immune globulin from a measured fetomaternal bleed.

props.label: Titers q4 → q2 wk · ≥ 2 dilutions = significant · critical → Doppler · anti-K lower
RhIG 300 µg = 30 mL WB / 15 mL RBC, ≤ 72 h · rosette + → KB or flow

explanation.what: Plain language: a mother’s IgG antibodies can cross the placenta and destroy her baby’s red cells; the lab measures the antibody, watches its strength and helps prevent anti-D with an injection. Scientific terms: HDFN, antibody titer, critical titer, middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity (MCA-PSV, MoM), Rh immune globulin (RhIG), fetomaternal hemorrhage (FMH), rosette test, Kleihauer–Betke test, flow cytometry for fetal cells, anti-G.
explanation.why: Maternal IgG crosses the placenta; IgM does not. Anti-K also targets erythroid progenitors, so anemia is earlier and occurs at lower titers. ABO HDFN needs IgG anti-A/B (typical of group O mothers) and is mild because fetal A/B antigens are weakly expressed. Anti-G recognises an epitope shared by D and C antigens.
explanation.measure: RhIG 300 µg (1500 IU) covers 30 mL fetal whole blood or 15 mL fetal RBCs (20 µg per mL fetal RBCs); postpartum within 72 h (up to 28 days if missed). Titers every 4 weeks to ~24 weeks, then every 2; test the previous sample in parallel; a ≥ 2-dilution change is significant. Critical titers are lab- and guideline-dependent (Valentini 2025 table: D/c > 32, Kell > 4; Jacobs 2025: anti-K ≥ 8). MCA-PSV > 1.5 MoM suggests fetal anemia. Rosette screen detects ~10 mL fetal whole blood; KB or flow cytometry (most accurate) quantify. Vials = FMH (mL whole blood) ÷ 30, rounded (up if ≥ 0.5), plus one extra vial per technical guidance (practice varies).
explanation.differs: Passive anti-D (after RhIG; up to ~8 weeks; falling) vs immune anti-D (stable or rising). Anti-G vs anti-D + anti-C (differential adsorption/elution). ABO HDFN (mild, weak DAT) vs Rh HDFN (strong DAT, can be severe).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: RhIG vial calculations, 72-hour window, significant titer change, anti-K erythropoietic suppression, rosette → KB/flow, anti-G and RhIG eligibility, and why ABO HDFN is mild.

comparisons.title: Anti-D vs anti-K in pregnancy
comparisons.distinguisher: Anti-K suppresses fetal erythropoiesis, so titers are interpreted at lower thresholds.

mnemonic.explanation: One RhIG vial covers 30 mL fetal whole blood or 15 mL red cells, given within 72 hours; anti-K suppresses fetal red-cell production.
mnemonic.limitation: A missed 72-hour window is not a reason to skip the dose (up to 28 days); large FMH needs extra vials; anti-K critical titers differ between guidelines.

The patients and titers are invented.

takeaway: Follow titers in parallel and act on a two-dilution rise or a critical titer, treat anti-K with a lower threshold, and dose Rh immune globulin from a measured fetomaternal bleed.

questions.stem: After delivery of a D-positive baby, a D-negative mother’s rosette screen is positive. What is the next step?

options.text: Quantify the fetomaternal hemorrhage by Kleihauer–Betke or flow cytometry and calculate the RhIG dose
options.rationale: Correct. A positive rosette screen means FMH above ~10 mL; quantitation determines how many vials are needed.

options.text: Give one standard vial; the rosette result does not change the dose
options.rationale: Incorrect. One vial covers only 30 mL fetal whole blood; larger bleeds need more.

options.text: Withhold RhIG because the mother is already immunised
options.rationale: Incorrect. The rosette detects fetal D-positive cells, not maternal anti-D.

options.text: Repeat the rosette screen in 72 hours
options.rationale: Incorrect. Waiting risks missing the 72-hour window; quantify now.

questions.stem: A D-negative woman’s anti-D titer was 8 at 20 weeks. At 24 weeks it is 32, tested in parallel with the stored 20-week sample. How should this be interpreted?

options.text: Significant rise (two dilutions); intensify surveillance and notify the obstetric team
options.rationale: Correct. A change of two or more dilutions tested in parallel is significant; at a critical titer, MCA Doppler follows.

options.text: Within test variation; repeat in four weeks
options.rationale: Incorrect. Variation is about one dilution; this is two.

options.text: Passive anti-D from RhIG; no action
options.rationale: Incorrect. Passive anti-D falls over time; this titer is rising.
Incorrect. Exchange transfusion is a neonatal treatment; antenatal surveillance comes first.

questions.stem: Why can anti-K cause severe fetal anemia at lower titers than anti-D?

options.text: Anti-K also suppresses fetal erythroid progenitors, not only mature red cells
options.rationale: Correct. Erythropoietic suppression adds to hemolysis, so anemia comes earlier and at lower titers.

options.text: Anti-K is IgM and crosses the placenta more easily
options.rationale: Incorrect. Clinically significant anti-K is IgG; IgM does not cross the placenta.

options.text: K antigen is expressed only on fetal red cells
options.rationale: Incorrect. K is expressed on adult red cells too; the difference is expression on early progenitors.
Incorrect. Anti-K titers are measured; they are interpreted at lower thresholds.

references.usedFor: 20 µg RhIG per mL fetal RBCs; 300 µg (1500 IU) vial covers 30 mL fetal whole blood or 15 mL fetal RBCs; SOGC: within 72 h, up to 28 days if missed; rosette test detects 5 mL fetal RBCs (10 mL whole blood), positive → quantitative testing; vials = mL WB/30, round up if ≥ 0.5, then add a vial (technical guidance; Canadian practice varies); KB labour-intensive and overestimates with high maternal F cells; flow cytometry most accurate.

references.citation: Visser GHA, Thommesen T, Di Renzo GC, et al. FIGO/ICM guidelines for preventing Rhesus disease: a call to action. Int J Gynaecol Obstet. 2021;152(2):144-147.
references.usedFor: 1500 IU (300 µg) within 72 h after delivery neutralizes 30 mL D-positive fetal whole blood; KB to estimate FMH volume.

references.citation: Valentini B, Ramirez Zegarra R, Ghi T, Dall’Asta A. Red blood cell alloimmunization and pregnancy: diagnosis and management. Pregnancy (Hoboken). 2025;1(5):e70085.
references.usedFor: Screen all women at first visit, D-negative retest 24–28 weeks; titers every 4 weeks until 24 (28) weeks then every 2 weeks; critical titer table (D/c > 1:32, C/E > 1:16, Kell > 1:4); MCA-PSV > 1.5 MoM → cordocentesis; anti-K suppresses fetal erythropoiesis via progenitors, earlier and more severe anemia, IUT at lower antibody levels; ABO HDFN rare and usually mild (0.3–0.8% Caucasian neonates), group O mothers, IgG anti-A/B, low fetal A/B expression; antenatal 300 µg at 28 weeks.

references.citation: Basu S, Kaur R, Kaur G. Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn: current trends and perspectives. Asian J Transfus Sci. 2011;5(1):3-7.
references.usedFor: Change of ≥ 2 dilutions significant; previous frozen sample tested in parallel; passive anti-D detectable by IAT up to ~8 weeks, immune anti-D detectable ~4 weeks after exposure and stable or rising; ABO HDFN almost exclusively in group A/B infants of group O mothers (IgG anti-A, anti-B); DAT weak or negative in ABO HDFN.

references.citation: Jacobs JW, Sugrue RP, Federspiel JJ, et al. The utility of a critical antibody titer in anti-K alloimmunized pregnancies: a systematic review and meta-analysis of diagnostic test accuracy. Transfus Med Rev. 2025;39(2):150895.
references.usedFor: Anti-K causes hemolysis and erythropoietic suppression; second most common cause of severe HDFN; titer ≥ 8 pooled sensitivity 97.0%, specificity 33.1%; 98.6% of severe cases at titers ≥ 8; guidelines historically avoided anti-K titers; practice varies.

references.citation: Makroo RN, Kaul A, Bhatia A, Agrawal S, Singh C, Karna P. Anti-G antibody in alloimmunized pregnant women: report of two cases. Asian J Transfus Sci. 2015;9(2):210-212.
references.usedFor: Apparent anti-D + anti-C may be anti-G or anti-G + C; can be mistaken for RhIG failure; a woman with anti-G alone can still be immunised to D and should receive RhIG; double/differential adsorption and elution with r′r′ and R0r cells.

claims.text: RhIG 300 µg covers 30 mL fetal WB / 15 mL RBCs; antenatal (often 28 weeks) and within 72 h postpartum (up to 28 days); passive anti-D up to ~8 weeks.
Screen first visit, D-negative 24–28 weeks; titers q4 → q2 weeks; parallel testing; ≥ 2-dilution change significant; critical titer → MCA-PSV; > 1.5 MoM → cordocentesis.
Anti-K suppresses erythroid progenitors; earlier anemia at lower titers; lower critical titers; 98.6% of severe cases at titer ≥ 8.
ABO HDFN almost only with group O mothers (IgG anti-A/B); usually mild from weak fetal A/B expression; DAT may be weak or negative.
Anti-G mimics anti-D + anti-C; adsorption/elution separates; anti-G alone still warrants RhIG.
Rosette detects ~10 mL fetal WB; positive → KB or flow; flow most accurate; KB overestimates with high maternal F cells; vials = mL WB ÷ 30, round, add one vial (technical guidance; practice varies).
Anti-C titer ≥ 4× anti-D suggests anti-G; severe ABO HDFN ~0.04%; exchange-transfusion bilirubin thresholds.

accuracyFlags.issue: Hit 10, Hit 15 and Trap 5 say anti-K titers underestimate risk and call for Doppler “regardless of titer.” Jacobs 2025 (meta-analysis) found 98.6% of severe anti-K HDFN at titers ≥ 8 and supports a critical titer; guidelines differ. The lesson teaches a lower anti-K threshold with close surveillance.
